The paper presents analytical models for predicting the spalling life of ceramic thermal barrier coatings (TBCs) used in aircraft gas turbine engines.

TBC spalling was attributed to a combination of mechanisms including metal oxidation, interface stress concentrations, interface stresses due to curvature and roughness, material properties, temperature gradients, and component design features.
The TBC failure models were developed based on observations of TBC failure modes and plausible failure theories.
TBC failure was assumed to occur when the imposed stresses exceeded the material strength near the ceramic-metal interface.
The authors note that TBC failure knowledge gaps exist due to a lack of experimental evidence and analytical understanding.
The analytical models are considered initial engineering approaches that capture observed TBC failure trends, rather than comprehensive predictive tools.
The paper discusses both electron beam-physical vapor deposited (EB-PVD) and plasma sprayed TBC systems.
The intent of the analytical models is to predict the spalling life of ceramic TBCs in aircraft gas turbine engines.
The authors highlight the need for further experimental data and improved analytical understanding to enhance the predictive capabilities of the TBC failure models.
